evidence.study_type: systematic review of randomized controlled trials
evidence.population: adults across randomized trials of oral magnesium as a stand-alone intervention
evidence.sample_size: 12 randomized trials in the main sleep/insomnia synthesis; 3 additional movement- or cramp-related trials analyzed separately
evidence.supported_claim_language: A 2026 systematic review of randomized trials found inconsistent effects of oral magnesium on sleep and rated the certainty of sleep-related evidence low to very low. The review did not support magnesium as a routine treatment for insomnia, while allowing that modest benefits on selected subjective outcomes remain possible in some adults.
evidence.evidence_grade: systematic review; low-to-very-low certainty by GRADE
evidence.safety_note: The review did not identify a clearly superior magnesium formulation, elemental dose, or treatment duration. Trial safety reporting was inconsistent and often short-term; individual use still requires attention to renal function, comorbidities, concomitant medicines, tolerability, and elemental magnesium content.

evidence.effect_or_condition: attention, acute stress, anxiety, depressive symptoms, fatigue, and short-term safety
evidence.study_type: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
evidence.population: healthy and clinical populations receiving oral L-theanine versus placebo
evidence.supported_claim_language: A 2026 meta-analysis of 31 randomized trials found that a single 200 mg L-theanine dose taken 30 to 60 minutes before testing improved choice reaction time in healthy adults (SMD 0.51, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.77). Acute stress reduction was modest and strongly influenced by high-risk-of-bias studies; fatigue did not improve significantly and anxiety effects were inconsistent.
evidence.safety_note: No serious adverse events were reported in the included randomized trials, but that finding does not establish long-term safety or exclude uncommon adverse effects and clinically important interactions. The review also reported an author conflict involving a supplement company.

evidence.study_type: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
evidence.population: human participants of varied ages and health status in randomized L-theanine supplementation trials reporting sleep outcomes
evidence.sample_size: 19 articles; 897 participants; 18 studies included in meta-analysis
evidence.supported_claim_language: A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis reported small improvements in subjective sleep-onset latency (SMD 0.15), daytime dysfunction (SMD 0.33), and overall subjective sleep quality (SMD 0.43) across randomized L-theanine supplementation trials.
evidence.safety_note: The evidence should not be converted into a universal insomnia-treatment, dose, or timing recommendation because studies differed in participants, formulations and intervention context, and the literature included a limited number of pure L-theanine trials.

evidence.effect_or_condition: depression, anxiety, and mood outcomes in adults
evidence.study_type: GRADE-assessed systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials
evidence.population: adults in randomized trials lasting at least four weeks with saffron as the sole intervention difference
evidence.supported_claim_language: A 2026 GRADE-assessed meta-analysis of 34 randomized trials found lower self-reported Beck Depression Inventory and Beck Anxiety Inventory scores with saffron, but clinician-rated HDRS and HARS outcomes and POMS were not significantly improved. Heterogeneity was very high for the BDI and BAI analyses, so self-report and clinician-rated findings should remain separate.
evidence.evidence_grade: systematic review/meta-analysis; moderate certainty by GRADE
evidence.safety_note: This synthesis supports outcome-specific evidence framing rather than a general antidepressant or anxiolytic equivalence claim. The high heterogeneity and disagreement between self-reported and clinician-rated scales require prominent uncertainty.
